Riverside Community Garden: Plot Renewal Notice

Current gardeners who wish to keep their plots for the coming season must submit a renewal form by February 15. Forms are available in the toolshed or on the garden's website.

Please note that plots showing little activity last season (for example, beds left unweeded for more than three weeks) will not be eligible for automatic renewal. Those gardeners will be placed on the general waiting list instead.

Questions may be directed to the garden coordinator at the toolshed on Saturday mornings.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, why are fungal hyphae able to gather resources that plant roots cannot?
passage:
Underground Partnerships

Most land plants do not absorb nutrients from the soil entirely on their own. Instead, their roots form partnerships with fungi known as mycorrhizae. The fungus grows thin threads, called hyphae, that spread far beyond the reach of the roots. Because these threads are much narrower than even the finest root hairs, they can penetrate tiny spaces between soil particles and collect water and minerals, especially phosphorus, that the plant could not otherwise obtain.

The arrangement benefits both partners. In exchange for minerals, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars produced during photosynthesis. Some estimates suggest that a plant may transfer up to a fifth of the carbon it fixes to its fungal partners. This is a considerable cost, but experiments show that plants grown in sterilized soil, where the fungi have been removed, often grow more slowly and are more vulnerable to drought.

Researchers have also found that hyphae can connect the roots of neighboring plants, forming extensive underground networks. Through these links, carbon and certain chemical signals may pass from one plant to another. For example, seedlings growing in deep shade sometimes receive carbon from taller trees nearby. prompt: According to paragraph 1, what can a bat learn from the echoes of its calls?
passage:
Hunting with Echoes

Many bats hunt at night, when vision is of little use. To find their way and locate prey, they rely on echolocation. A bat produces short, high-pitched calls, most of which are far above the range of human hearing. When these sound waves strike an object, such as a moth or a branch, part of the sound bounces back. By analyzing the returning echoes, the bat can judge the object's distance, size, and even its texture.

The timing of the echo is especially important. Because sound travels at a fairly steady speed through air, a longer delay between a call and its echo indicates a more distant object. As a bat closes in on an insect, it calls more and more rapidly, sometimes producing over a hundred calls per second just before capture. This final burst of sound, known as the feeding buzz, gives the bat constantly updated information about the insect's position.

Some insects have evolved defenses against this hunting strategy. Certain moths possess ears that can detect bat calls, allowing them to dive or fly erratically when a bat approaches. A few species of tiger moth go further, producing clicking sounds of their own. These clicks may warn bats that the moth tastes unpleasant, or they may interfere with the bat's ability to interpret its echoes.

The color and temperature of an object
The age and species of other nearby bats
The direction of the wind and coming weather

explanation: Paragraph 1 states that echoes let the bat judge an object's distance, size, and texture.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what do corals provide to the algae living in their tissues?
passage:
Why Corals Turn White

Reef-building corals may look like rocks or plants, but they are animals. Each coral colony consists of thousands of tiny individuals called polyps, which build hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. Living inside the tissues of most of these polyps are single-celled algae. The algae carry out photosynthesis and pass much of the food they produce to their hosts. In return, the corals provide the algae with shelter and with nutrients from their waste. The algae also give corals much of their color.

This relationship is sensitive to temperature. When seawater stays only one or two degrees Celsius above its usual summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership begins to break down. Stressed corals expel their algae, and because the coral tissue itself is nearly transparent, the white skeleton becomes visible underneath. This process is known as bleaching.

Bleaching does not necessarily mean that a coral is dead. If water temperatures return to normal fairly quickly, the corals can take in new algae and gradually recover. However, without its algae, a coral loses its main source of food, and prolonged bleaching often leads to starvation and disease. Because large bleaching events have become more frequent, scientists are studying whether some types of algae are more tolerant of heat and might help reefs survive warmer conditions.

Calcium carbonate for building skeletons
Shelter and nutrients from the corals' waste
Color that protects them from sunlight

explanation: Paragraph 1 states that corals give the algae shelter and nutrients from their waste.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what does a forager do during the waggle run?
passage:
The Language of the Hive

When a honeybee forager discovers a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and shares its location with her nestmates through a remarkable series of movements called the waggle dance. The dance is performed on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, usually in the darkness of the hive. The forager runs forward in a straight line while shaking her abdomen from side to side, then circles back to her starting point and repeats the run.

Two features of the dance carry most of the information. The first is the angle of the straight run. Bees treat straight up on the comb as the direction of the sun, so a run angled forty degrees to the right of vertical tells other bees to fly forty degrees to the right of the sun. The second is the duration of the waggle run: the longer the run lasts, the farther away the food source is.

Because other workers cannot see the dancer clearly in the dark, they follow her closely, detecting her movements through touch and the vibrations she produces. They also pick up the scent of the flowers clinging to her body. Interestingly, studies have shown that recruits often need several trips before they find the advertised site, suggesting that the dance provides a general direction rather than a precise map.

She moves in a straight line while shaking her abdomen.
She leaves flower scent at the edges of the comb.
She taps the other workers with her front legs.

explanation: Paragraph 1 says the forager runs forward in a straight line while shaking her abdomen from side to side.

prompt: Why does the author mention birds and mammals in paragraph 1?
passage:
Seeds Carried by Ants

Plants cannot move, yet many of them rely on animals to carry their seeds to new places. Birds and mammals that eat fruit are the best-known seed dispersers, but thousands of plant species depend on a much smaller partner: the ant. This relationship, called myrmecochory, is especially common in the dry shrublands of Australia and South Africa and in the forests of eastern North America.

Seeds dispersed by ants carry a small attachment called an elaiosome, a fatty structure rich in nutrients. Worker ants pick up the seed, using the elaiosome as a convenient handle, and carry it back to their nest. There, the elaiosome is removed and fed to the colony's larvae. The seed itself, which is hard and difficult for ants to damage, is then discarded, either in an underground waste chamber or outside the nest entrance.

For the plant, this treatment provides several advantages. Seeds are moved away from the parent plant, which reduces competition between parent and offspring. Seeds buried in the nest are also hidden from rodents and birds that would otherwise eat them. In addition, ant waste chambers tend to be rich in nutrients, offering seedlings a favorable place to grow. In fire-prone habitats, buried seeds are also protected from the intense heat that destroys seeds lying on the surface.

prompt: Why does the author begin by stating that bacteria were once regarded as solitary organisms?
passage:
Bacteria That Count

For much of the twentieth century, bacteria were regarded as solitary organisms, each cell acting independently of its neighbors. This view was challenged by research on Vibrio fischeri, a marine bacterium that produces light. Investigators noticed that the bacteria glowed brightly when densely packed but remained dark when dispersed in open seawater. The explanation proved to be a process now called quorum sensing.

Each bacterial cell releases small signaling molecules known as autoinducers. When cells are sparse, these molecules diffuse away and their concentration stays low. As a population grows within a confined space, however, the molecules accumulate until they cross a threshold concentration. At that point, they bind to receptor proteins inside the cells and switch on particular genes, in this case those responsible for light production. The behavior is thus triggered not by any single cell but by the population as a whole.

Such coordination makes sense for activities that are futile when attempted alone. A lone glowing cell would be invisible and merely squander energy, whereas billions glowing at once produce a useful effect. In the Hawaiian bobtail squid, which houses V. fischeri in a special organ, the glow is thought to hide the squid's shadow from predators below on moonlit nights. Quorum sensing has since been found in many disease-causing bacteria, some of which delay releasing toxins until their numbers can overwhelm a host's defenses.

To argue that early microbiologists ignored marine bacteria entirely

explanation: The author presents the older view and then says it was challenged by research on Vibrio fischeri.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what is the "difficult trade-off" faced by large desert mammals?
passage:
Keeping Cool in the Desert

Large mammals living in hot deserts face a difficult trade-off. The most effective way to shed excess heat is to evaporate water, by sweating or panting, yet water is precisely the resource a desert animal can least afford to lose. The dromedary camel resolves this conflict in part through a strategy called adaptive heterothermy. Rather than holding its body temperature nearly constant, as most mammals do, a dehydrated camel allows its temperature to rise by as much as six degrees Celsius over the course of a hot day.

This tolerance yields two benefits. First, heat that would otherwise have to be removed by evaporation is simply stored in the body and released at night, when the air is cool, by conduction and radiation. Second, a warmer body narrows the difference between the animal's temperature and that of the surrounding air, so less heat flows into the camel from its environment. Calculations suggest that a large camel can save several liters of water per day in this way.

The camel's nose contributes as well. Its nasal passages are lined with elaborate folded surfaces. When the animal exhales, moisture in the warm breath condenses on these cooler surfaces and is reabsorbed rather than lost to the atmosphere. Notably, these adjustments are most pronounced when water is scarce; a well-watered camel regulates its temperature much like other mammals.

explanation: Paragraph 1 explains that evaporating water is the most effective cooling method, yet water is what desert animals can least afford to lose.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what distinguishes a keystone species?
passage:
Otters, Urchins, and Kelp

In the late 1960s, ecologists coined the term keystone species to describe organisms whose influence on an ecosystem is far greater than their abundance would suggest. Among the most cited examples is the sea otter of the North Pacific. Sea otters feed heavily on sea urchins, which in turn graze on kelp, the large brown algae that form dense underwater forests.

The importance of this chain of interactions became evident through a kind of unplanned experiment. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, otters were hunted for their fur until they had vanished from much of their range. Where otters disappeared, urchin populations expanded unchecked and consumed kelp so thoroughly that forests gave way to barren stretches of rock covered with urchins. Where otters survived or were later reintroduced, kelp forests persisted, along with the fish, invertebrates, and seabirds that depend on them. Because the predator's effect passes down through two feeding levels, such a pattern is called a trophic cascade.

Subsequent research has complicated this tidy picture. Kelp forests are also shaped by water temperature, storms, and nutrient supply, and in some regions urchin numbers are controlled by disease or by other predators, such as large sea stars. Nevertheless, comparisons of coastlines with and without otters consistently reveal striking differences, and the otter remains a compelling illustration of how removing a single species can reorganize an entire community.

It feeds on more kinds of prey than any other local species.
It was the first species in its habitat to be studied closely.

explanation: Paragraph 1 defines keystone species as organisms whose influence is far greater than their abundance would suggest.

prompt: The word "compelling" in the passage is closest in meaning to
passage:
Otters, Urchins, and Kelp

In the late 1960s, ecologists coined the term keystone species to describe organisms whose influence on an ecosystem is far greater than their abundance would suggest. Among the most cited examples is the sea otter of the North Pacific. Sea otters feed heavily on sea urchins, which in turn graze on kelp, the large brown algae that form dense underwater forests.

The importance of this chain of interactions became evident through a kind of unplanned experiment. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, otters were hunted for their fur until they had vanished from much of their range. Where otters disappeared, urchin populations expanded unchecked and consumed kelp so thoroughly that forests gave way to barren stretches of rock covered with urchins. Where otters survived or were later reintroduced, kelp forests persisted, along with the fish, invertebrates, and seabirds that depend on them. Because the predator's effect passes down through two feeding levels, such a pattern is called a trophic cascade.

Subsequent research has complicated this tidy picture. Kelp forests are also shaped by water temperature, storms, and nutrient supply, and in some regions urchin numbers are controlled by disease or by other predators, such as large sea stars. Nevertheless, comparisons of coastlines with and without otters consistently reveal striking differences, and the otter remains a compelling illustration of how removing a single species can reorganize an entire community.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, why is rubisco described as inefficient?
passage:
A More Efficient Leaf

Nearly all plants capture carbon dioxide with the help of an enzyme called rubisco, which is probably the most abundant protein on Earth. Despite its central role, rubisco is surprisingly inefficient. In addition to carbon dioxide, it readily binds oxygen, triggering a wasteful process known as photorespiration that releases previously fixed carbon. The problem worsens at high temperatures, when rubisco's preference for carbon dioxide declines and leaves, closing their pores to conserve water, allow oxygen to build up inside.

Some plants, including maize, sugarcane, and many tropical grasses, have evolved a solution called C4 photosynthesis. In these species, carbon dioxide is first captured in the outer cells of the leaf by a different enzyme that does not react with oxygen. The resulting four-carbon compound is then shuttled into an inner ring of cells surrounding the leaf veins, where it is broken down to release carbon dioxide. Rubisco is confined to these inner cells, so it works where carbon dioxide is highly concentrated and photorespiration is suppressed.

This arrangement is not free; pumping carbon dioxide inward consumes additional energy. As a result, C4 plants hold a clear advantage in hot, sunny, and dry habitats but tend to be outcompeted in cool, shaded ones. The C4 pathway has arisen independently more than sixty times in different plant lineages, which suggests that it is an accessible evolutionary path when conditions favor it.

It reacts with oxygen as well as with carbon dioxide.
It requires high temperatures to bind carbon dioxide.

explanation: Paragraph 1 explains that rubisco readily binds oxygen, triggering wasteful photorespiration.

prompt: According to paragraph 2, how did researchers show that robins use a magnetic compass?
passage:
A Compass in the Eye

Each autumn, many songbirds fly thousands of kilometers to their wintering grounds, often at night over unfamiliar terrain. How they maintain their heading has long puzzled biologists. Birds are known to use several cues, including the position of the sun and the patterns of stars, but one of the most intriguing is Earth's magnetic field.

Evidence for a magnetic compass came from experiments in the 1960s with European robins. During the migratory season, caged robins hop restlessly in the direction they would normally fly. When researchers placed the cages inside coils that shifted the direction of the magnetic field, the birds shifted their orientation accordingly. Further tests produced an unexpected result: the birds did not distinguish magnetic north from magnetic south. Instead, they appeared to sense the angle at which field lines dip toward the ground, which differs between the poleward and equatorward directions. The robins' compass therefore works differently from a human-made one.

How birds detect the field remains debated. One leading hypothesis holds that light-sensitive proteins in the eye undergo chemical reactions influenced by magnetic fields, perhaps allowing birds to perceive the field as a pattern overlaid on their vision. Consistent with this idea, the robins' compass appears to require light of certain wavelengths. Other researchers have proposed that iron-containing particles in the beak region serve as magnetic sensors, and birds may use more than one mechanism.

choices.text: By altering the field around the cages and observing the birds' orientation
By releasing robins at night and tracking them across unfamiliar terrain
By covering the cages so that the birds could not see the stars
By attaching small magnets to the birds and comparing their flight paths

sampleAnswer: By altering the field around the cages and observing the birds' orientation
explanation: Paragraph 2 says that when coils shifted the field direction, the birds shifted their orientation accordingly.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, where does much of the carbon dioxide absorbed by rainwater come from?
passage:
How Limestone Caves Form

Most of the world's large caves form in limestone, a sedimentary rock composed largely of calcium carbonate. Although limestone appears solid and durable, it is vulnerable to a slow chemical attack. As rain falls through the atmosphere and then percolates through soil, it absorbs carbon dioxide, much of it released by decaying plant matter. The result is a weak solution of carbonic acid, which gradually dissolves calcium carbonate as it seeps into cracks in the rock.

Over thousands of years, this process widens the original fractures into channels. Dissolution is most rapid near the water table, where groundwater moves horizontally and constantly brings fresh acidic water into contact with the rock. For this reason, many cave systems consist of long, nearly level passages arranged in distinct tiers. Each tier is thought to mark a former position of the water table, which dropped as nearby rivers cut their valleys deeper.

Once a passage is drained and filled with air, a reverse process can begin. Water dripping from the ceiling releases some of its dissolved carbon dioxide into the cave air, and as a result it can no longer hold all of its calcium carbonate. The mineral is deposited as stalactites and other formations, so caves are simultaneously products of erosion and sites of new rock growth.

Decaying plant material in the soil
Seawater that floods low-lying caves
Chemical reactions inside stalactites

explanation: Paragraph 1 states that the carbon dioxide is largely released by decaying plant matter in the soil.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, all of the following help explain why water warms more slowly than land EXCEPT:
passage:
Sea Breezes and Land Breezes

On many coastlines, a cool wind begins blowing in from the sea by late morning on sunny days and fades after sunset. This sea breeze is a small-scale circulation driven by the different ways land and water respond to sunlight. Land surfaces heat up quickly because sunlight is absorbed in a thin top layer and soil has a relatively low heat capacity. Water, by contrast, warms slowly: sunlight penetrates several meters, waves and currents mix the heat downward, and water requires more energy than soil to raise its temperature by the same amount.

As the land warms, the air above it expands and rises, lowering the air pressure near the ground. Cooler, denser air over the sea flows inland to replace it, producing the breeze. Aloft, the rising air drifts back out over the water and sinks, completing a loop. The leading edge of the incoming marine air, called the sea-breeze front, can push tens of kilometers inland and sometimes triggers afternoon thunderstorms where it lifts warm, moist air.

At night the pattern reverses. Land loses heat rapidly by radiation, while the sea stays comparatively warm, so a land breeze flows offshore. Because the temperature contrast is usually smaller at night, land breezes are generally gentler than their daytime counterparts.

prompt: According to paragraph 2, what happens to the air that rises over the warm land?
passage:
Sea Breezes and Land Breezes

On many coastlines, a cool wind begins blowing in from the sea by late morning on sunny days and fades after sunset. This sea breeze is a small-scale circulation driven by the different ways land and water respond to sunlight. Land surfaces heat up quickly because sunlight is absorbed in a thin top layer and soil has a relatively low heat capacity. Water, by contrast, warms slowly: sunlight penetrates several meters, waves and currents mix the heat downward, and water requires more energy than soil to raise its temperature by the same amount.

As the land warms, the air above it expands and rises, lowering the air pressure near the ground. Cooler, denser air over the sea flows inland to replace it, producing the breeze. Aloft, the rising air drifts back out over the water and sinks, completing a loop. The leading edge of the incoming marine air, called the sea-breeze front, can push tens of kilometers inland and sometimes triggers afternoon thunderstorms where it lifts warm, moist air.

At night the pattern reverses. Land loses heat rapidly by radiation, while the sea stays comparatively warm, so a land breeze flows offshore. Because the temperature contrast is usually smaller at night, land breezes are generally gentler than their daytime counterparts.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, when does a comet become visible from Earth?
passage:
The Tails of Comets

A comet spends most of its orbit far from the Sun as a frozen nucleus only a few kilometers across, made of ice, dust, and rocky fragments. Astronomers often describe such a nucleus as a dirty snowball. Only when its orbit carries it into the inner solar system does a comet develop the glowing features that make it visible from Earth.

As the nucleus warms, its ices turn directly into gas, a process called sublimation, releasing dust grains that were trapped inside. The gas and dust form a vast, hazy cloud, or coma, that can grow larger than a planet. From the coma, two distinct tails usually stream away. The dust tail is broad, curved, and yellowish, because the grains reflect sunlight and are pushed gently outward by the pressure of light itself. The ion tail is narrow, straight, and often bluish. It consists of gas molecules that have been electrically charged by solar ultraviolet light and are swept along by the solar wind, a stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun.

Because both forces originate at the Sun, a comet's tails point away from the Sun rather than trailing behind the comet along its path. As a comet moves outward after its closest approach, its tails actually travel ahead of it.

explanation: Paragraph 1 says the comet develops its glowing, visible features only in the inner solar system.

prompt: Why does the author mention Peru, California, and Namibia?
passage:
Coastal Upwelling

Some of the most productive fishing grounds on Earth lie off the western coasts of continents, in places such as Peru, California, and Namibia. Their richness results from upwelling, a process that brings cold water from depth up to the sunlit surface.

Upwelling begins with wind. Along these coasts, prevailing winds blow roughly parallel to the shoreline, toward the equator. Because of Earth's rotation, however, the surface water set in motion does not simply follow the wind. In the Northern Hemisphere it is deflected to the right, and in the Southern Hemisphere to the left, so that the net movement of the upper layer is directed away from the coast. As surface water is pushed offshore, deeper water rises to take its place.

This deep water is cold, but it is also loaded with nitrates, phosphates, and other nutrients released as organic matter decayed while sinking through the ocean. Once these nutrients reach the surface, microscopic algae called phytoplankton multiply rapidly, supporting dense populations of small fish such as anchovies and sardines, which in turn feed seabirds, marine mammals, and larger fish. Upwelling zones cover only a tiny fraction of the ocean's surface, yet they account for a remarkably large share of the global fish catch. When the winds weaken, as happens periodically off Peru, upwelling slows and fisheries can decline sharply.

prompt: Why does the author mention that lakes freeze from the top down?
passage:
Why Ice Floats

For most substances, the solid form is denser than the liquid, so a chunk of the solid sinks in its own melt. Water is a striking exception. Ice is about nine percent less dense than liquid water, which is why ice cubes float in a glass and lakes freeze from the top down.

The explanation lies in the structure of the water molecule. Each molecule consists of one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, and the oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself. As a result, the oxygen end carries a slight negative charge and the hydrogen ends carry slight positive charges. The positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the negative oxygen of a neighbor, forming what is called a hydrogen bond.

In liquid water, these bonds constantly break and re-form, allowing molecules to crowd closely together. When water freezes, however, each molecule becomes locked into hydrogen bonds with four neighbors, arranged in an open, six-sided lattice containing considerable empty space. This rigid framework holds the molecules farther apart than in the liquid, lowering the density. The consequences are significant for living things. Because floating ice insulates the water beneath it, lakes and ponds rarely freeze solid in winter, and fish and other aquatic organisms can survive in the liquid layer below.

To show that most liquids behave the same way as water

explanation: Lakes freezing from the top is given as an example of what happens because ice floats.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, how does the mantle behave over geologic time?
passage:
Postglacial Rebound

During the last glacial period, ice sheets up to three kilometers thick covered much of Canada and Scandinavia. Their immense weight did more than scour the landscape; it pressed the underlying crust downward into the mantle. Although the mantle is solid rock, over geologic time it behaves like an extremely viscous fluid, slowly flowing away from regions under load. The crust, in effect, floats on this deformable layer, a state of balance that geologists call isostasy.

When the ice sheets melted at the close of the glacial period, the load was removed, but the crust did not spring back immediately. Because mantle rock flows so sluggishly, the land has been rising ever since and continues to do so today. Around the northern Gulf of Bothnia, uplift still exceeds eight millimeters per year. Evidence of this ongoing rebound is visible in raised beaches, ancient shorelines now stranded well above present sea level, and in harbors that have had to be dredged or relocated as the water grew shallower.

The phenomenon has scientific value beyond its local effects. By comparing rates of uplift with the size and timing of former ice sheets, researchers can estimate the viscosity of the mantle, a property that cannot be measured directly. Rebound also complicates the interpretation of tide-gauge records, since a gauge on rising land registers less sea-level rise than the global average.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, why is parallax limited as a method of measuring distance?
passage:
Cepheid Variables as Standard Candles

Measuring distances to remote objects is one of astronomy's most persistent challenges. Parallax, the apparent shift of a nearby star against more distant background stars as Earth orbits the Sun, works well for close stars, but beyond a certain range the shift becomes too small to detect. To reach farther, astronomers rely on standard candles: objects whose true brightness can be determined independently of their distance.

The most historically important standard candles are Cepheid variables, giant stars that brighten and dim in a regular cycle lasting from about a day to several months. In the early twentieth century, Henrietta Leavitt, studying many such stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, noticed that the brighter Cepheids had longer periods. Because all the stars in that cloud lie at roughly the same distance from Earth, differences in their apparent brightness reflected genuine differences in their luminosity. Leavitt had uncovered a period-luminosity relationship.

The implication was profound. By timing a Cepheid's cycle, an astronomer could infer its luminosity; comparing that value with how bright the star appears from Earth then yields its distance, since light dims predictably with distance. Later, Cepheids observed in the Andromeda nebula demonstrated that it lay far outside the Milky Way, establishing that our galaxy is only one of many. Calibrating the relationship, however, required independent distances to nearby Cepheids, which is why parallax remained essential.

For distant stars, the apparent shift is too small to detect.

explanation: Paragraph 1 says that beyond a certain range the parallax shift becomes too small to detect.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, why can annual layers not be counted in central Antarctica?
passage:
Climate Records in Polar Ice

The ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland preserve one of the most detailed records of Earth's past climate. Each year, snow accumulates on the surface and is compressed by later layers into glacial ice. Where snowfall is high, annual layers remain distinguishable, much like tree rings, allowing scientists to count back through time. Where accumulation is low, as in central Antarctica, the layers are too thin to count, and ages must instead be estimated by modeling how the ice flows and thins with depth.

Two kinds of evidence make these cores valuable. First, the ratio of heavy to light isotopes of oxygen and hydrogen in the ice reflects the temperature at which the snow formed; colder conditions yield snow depleted in the heavier isotopes. Second, as snow turns to ice, small bubbles become sealed inside, trapping samples of the ancient atmosphere. Analyzing these bubbles allows researchers to reconstruct past concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane directly.

Compared side by side, the two records reveal a close correspondence: during cold glacial periods greenhouse gas concentrations were low, and during warm interglacials they were higher. The correlation alone does not establish which change came first, and interpreting the timing is complicated because the air in the bubbles is younger than the surrounding ice. Air continues to circulate through porous snow until it is buried deeply enough to be sealed.

explanation: Paragraph 1 says accumulation is low in central Antarctica, making layers too thin to count.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what happens when a deformed nickel-titanium wire is gently heated?
passage:
Shape-Memory Alloys

Most metals, once bent beyond a certain point, stay bent. Shape-memory alloys behave differently. A wire made of nickel-titanium, the most widely used such alloy, can be deformed at room temperature and then, when gently heated, return precisely to its original form. This seemingly magical behavior arises from a reversible change in the alloy's crystal structure.

At higher temperatures, nickel-titanium adopts a highly ordered structure called austenite. When it cools, it transforms into a phase called martensite, whose crystals can shift into many slightly different orientations without breaking atomic bonds. Deforming the cooled alloy simply rearranges these orientations to accommodate the new shape. On heating, the martensite reverts to austenite, which has only one possible arrangement, so the metal is forced back into the configuration it held before cooling. The temperature at which this reversal occurs can be tuned by adjusting the ratio of nickel to titanium, sometimes by a fraction of a percent.

A related property, superelasticity, appears when the alloy is used slightly above its transformation temperature. Here, stress itself triggers the formation of martensite, allowing the material to stretch several percent and then spring back once the load is removed, far beyond the recoverable strain of ordinary steel. These properties have found applications ranging from medical stents, which are compressed for insertion and then expand inside a blood vessel, to eyeglass frames that resist permanent bending.

prompt: What can be inferred about adjusting the ratio of nickel to titanium?
passage:
Shape-Memory Alloys

Most metals, once bent beyond a certain point, stay bent. Shape-memory alloys behave differently. A wire made of nickel-titanium, the most widely used such alloy, can be deformed at room temperature and then, when gently heated, return precisely to its original form. This seemingly magical behavior arises from a reversible change in the alloy's crystal structure.

At higher temperatures, nickel-titanium adopts a highly ordered structure called austenite. When it cools, it transforms into a phase called martensite, whose crystals can shift into many slightly different orientations without breaking atomic bonds. Deforming the cooled alloy simply rearranges these orientations to accommodate the new shape. On heating, the martensite reverts to austenite, which has only one possible arrangement, so the metal is forced back into the configuration it held before cooling. The temperature at which this reversal occurs can be tuned by adjusting the ratio of nickel to titanium, sometimes by a fraction of a percent.

A related property, superelasticity, appears when the alloy is used slightly above its transformation temperature. Here, stress itself triggers the formation of martensite, allowing the material to stretch several percent and then spring back once the load is removed, far beyond the recoverable strain of ordinary steel. These properties have found applications ranging from medical stents, which are compressed for insertion and then expand inside a blood vessel, to eyeglass frames that resist permanent bending.

prompt: According to paragraph 2, what condition produces Rayleigh scattering?
passage:
The Color of the Sky

Sunlight looks white because it mixes all visible wavelengths. Yet the daytime sky is blue, and the Sun near the horizon looks orange or red. Both effects arise from how light interacts with air molecules.

Nitrogen and oxygen molecules are far smaller than the wavelengths of visible light. When light encounters such tiny particles, some of it is redirected in all directions, a process known as Rayleigh scattering. The strength of this scattering depends steeply on wavelength: it is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength. Because blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, it is scattered several times more strongly. As a result, blue light is redistributed across the whole sky and reaches an observer from every direction, while longer wavelengths tend to travel straight from the Sun. Violet light is scattered even more than blue, but the sky does not look violet, partly because sunlight contains less violet and partly because human eyes are less sensitive to it.

At sunrise and sunset, sunlight must cross a much longer path through the atmosphere to reach an observer. Along the way, most of the blue light is scattered out of the direct beam, leaving the remaining light dominated by orange and red. Larger particles, such as water droplets in clouds, scatter all wavelengths about equally, which is why clouds appear white or gray rather than blue.

Light with wavelengths longer than those of red light

explanation: Paragraph 2 describes Rayleigh scattering as occurring when light meets particles far smaller than its wavelength.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what did early experiments on memory show?
passage:
The Spacing Effect

For more than a century, psychologists have known that when people study matters as much as how long they study. In early experiments, researchers asked participants to memorize lists of unfamiliar syllables. Some participants reviewed the material in one long session, while others divided the same amount of practice across several days. When tested later, the second group remembered far more. This pattern, known as the spacing effect, has since been confirmed with vocabulary, historical facts, motor skills, and even the procedures used by medical trainees.

Why should spreading out practice be so helpful? One explanation focuses on forgetting. When a learner returns to material after a delay, some of it has begun to fade, so recalling it requires effort. That effort appears to strengthen the memory more than an easy review would. In contrast, repeating information that is still fresh in mind feels productive but adds little lasting benefit.

Despite this evidence, many students continue to cram before exams. Part of the reason is that cramming often works in the short term: a student who studies intensively the night before may perform reasonably well the next morning. The weakness of this approach becomes apparent only weeks later, when much of the information has disappeared. Because learners rarely notice what they have lost, they tend to underestimate the value of spacing.

choices.text: Participants learned unfamiliar syllables faster than familiar words.
Participants who studied in one long session remembered more.
Participants forgot syllables more slowly than historical facts.
Participants who spread practice over several days remembered more.

sampleAnswer: Participants who spread practice over several days remembered more.
explanation: The passage states that the group dividing practice across several days remembered far more when tested later.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what do traditional economic models assume about buyers?
passage:
Anchoring and Price

Traditional economic models assume that buyers judge a product's value by comparing its price with the benefits it offers. Research in behavioral economics, however, suggests that people's sense of what something is worth can be shaped by numbers that have little to do with the product itself. This tendency is called anchoring: an initial figure serves as a reference point, and later judgments are adjusted from it, usually not far enough.

In a typical laboratory study, participants are first asked whether they would pay a certain amount for an item, such as a bottle of olive oil or a textbook, and then asked to state the most they would actually pay. When the first amount is high, the final answers tend to be high as well, even when participants are told that the initial number was chosen at random. The anchor, in other words, influences decisions even when people know it is meaningless.

Retailers have long made use of this effect. A store may display an expensive model next to a moderately priced one, not because it expects to sell many of the costly items, but because the high price makes the second option seem reasonable. Similarly, a tag showing an "original" price beside a sale price invites shoppers to evaluate the discount rather than the actual cost.

They rely mainly on the first price they happen to see.
They prefer products that are offered at a discount.
They judge value by comparing prices across many stores.

explanation: Paragraph 1 states that traditional models assume buyers compare a product's price with its benefits.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what did the study of professional workers find?
passage:
The Strength of Weak Ties

When people look for work, they often turn to their closest friends and relatives for help. It might seem reasonable to expect that these strong ties would be the most useful sources of job information. Yet a well-known sociological study of professional workers in the 1970s found something surprising: most respondents who had found jobs through personal contacts had heard about the opening from acquaintances, people they saw only occasionally, rather than from close friends.

Sociologists explain this pattern by looking at the structure of social networks. Close friends tend to know one another and to move in the same circles, so the information they possess largely overlaps with what a person already knows. Acquaintances, by contrast, belong to different groups. They work for other employers, live in other neighborhoods, and hear news that would not otherwise reach the job seeker. Weak ties therefore act as bridges between otherwise separate clusters of people.

This idea has influenced research far beyond the job market. Studies of how new products, rumors, and innovations spread have shown that weak ties often carry information across a community more quickly than strong ties do. The insight suggests that a person's usefulness to others may depend less on the closeness of a relationship than on his or her position in a network.

Close friends were the most common source of information about jobs.

explanation: The study found that most respondents who used contacts heard about openings from acquaintances rather than close friends.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, why were most cities compact before the late nineteenth century?
passage:
Streetcar Suburbs

Before the late nineteenth century, most American cities were compact. Because the majority of residents traveled on foot, homes, shops, and workplaces had to be located within a short walk of one another, and wealthy and working families often lived on the same crowded streets. The introduction of electric streetcars in the late 1880s changed this arrangement dramatically.

Streetcars could carry passengers several miles in the time it once took to walk a single mile. Developers quickly recognized the opportunity. They purchased inexpensive farmland at the edge of the city, built streetcar lines out to it, and sold house lots to families eager to escape the noise and congestion of the center. Because riders needed to walk to the nearest stop, these new neighborhoods took a distinctive shape: narrow strips of housing stretched along the tracks, with small stores clustered at the stops.

The streetcar suburbs also contributed to a sorting of urban populations. A daily fare that was affordable for a clerk might be too expensive for a factory laborer, so outer neighborhoods tended to attract middle-class households, while poorer workers remained closer to the industrial core. In this way, a new transportation technology reshaped not only the physical form of cities but also their social geography.

choices.text: Wealthy families preferred to live near their workplaces.
Most residents had to walk wherever they went.
Land at the edge of cities was too costly to buy.
City governments limited how far streets could extend.

sampleAnswer: Most residents had to walk wherever they went.
explanation: Paragraph 1 explains that because most residents traveled on foot, everything had to be within a short walk.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what have education researchers noticed about peer tutoring?
passage:
Learning by Teaching

Peer tutoring programs are usually created to help students who are having difficulty with a subject. Over the past several decades, however, education researchers have noticed that the tutors themselves frequently benefit as much as the students they assist. In some studies, tutors showed greater improvement on later tests than their tutees did, even though they had begun with a stronger understanding of the material.

Several factors seem to account for this result. Preparing to teach encourages students to organize information more carefully than they would if they were studying only for themselves. They anticipate questions, look for clear examples, and identify gaps in their own knowledge. Explaining a concept aloud also forces tutors to put vague ideas into precise words, and when a tutee is confused, the tutor must find a second or third way of presenting the same point.

Interestingly, some of the benefit appears even before any teaching occurs. In laboratory experiments, students who were told they would later teach a passage to someone else remembered it better than students who expected only to take a test on it, although both groups studied for the same amount of time. Simply adopting the mindset of a teacher, it seems, changes the way people process new information.

choices.text: Tutees usually improve more quickly than their tutors.
Tutors often benefit as much as the students they help.
Tutoring works best when tutors and tutees are equally skilled.
Tutoring programs rarely help students with real difficulties.

sampleAnswer: Tutors often benefit as much as the students they help.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states that tutors frequently benefit as much as the students they assist.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, which of the following is true of a pidgin?
passage:
From Pidgin to Creole

When speakers of mutually unintelligible languages come into sustained contact, for instance through trade or plantation labor, they sometimes develop a simplified means of communication known as a pidgin. A pidgin typically draws most of its vocabulary from one dominant language, while its grammar is drastically reduced: verbs may lack tense endings, nouns may lack plural markers, and word order tends to be rigid. Crucially, a pidgin has no native speakers; it is a second language used for limited purposes.

The situation changes when children are raised in a community where a pidgin is the principal shared language. Exposed to input that is inconsistent and incomplete, these children do not merely reproduce what they hear. Instead, within one or two generations, they elaborate it into a fully expressive language, termed a creole, with systematic ways of marking time, aspect, and complex sentence structure.

This transformation has attracted scholarly interest because it seems to offer a window onto the human capacity for language. Some linguists have argued that the striking grammatical similarities among creoles that arose independently reflect an innate blueprint that children impose when their input is impoverished. Others contend that these resemblances can be traced to the languages spoken by the original adult populations, whose structures were carried over into the new varieties. The debate remains unresolved, partly because historical records of early creole communities are often sparse.

choices.text: It takes its vocabulary equally from all the languages in contact.
It is used as a second language rather than learned from birth.
It has a more flexible word order than the languages it comes from.
It is used for the full range of purposes in a community.

sampleAnswer: It is used as a second language rather than learned from birth.
explanation: Paragraph 1 states that a pidgin has no native speakers and is a second language used for limited purposes.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, how is refusing a gift viewed in the system described?
passage:
The Obligations of the Gift

In many societies, the exchange of gifts is far more than an expression of personal generosity. Early twentieth-century anthropologists, comparing accounts from Polynesia, Melanesia, and northwestern North America, argued that gifts are embedded in a system of three interlocking obligations: the obligation to give, the obligation to receive, and the obligation to reciprocate. Refusing a gift, in this view, is not a neutral act but a rejection of the social relationship it proposes, and failing to return one in due course can bring a loss of standing.

A celebrated example comes from the islands off the eastern tip of New Guinea, where men traditionally undertook long canoe voyages to exchange shell necklaces and armbands with partners on other islands. The objects had little practical use, and no participant kept them permanently; necklaces circulated in one direction around the ring of islands and armbands in the other. What the exchange produced, rather, was a durable web of partnerships that also facilitated more ordinary trade and cooperation.

Such cases have led scholars to distinguish gift economies from market exchange. In a market transaction, payment settles the account, and buyer and seller owe each other nothing further. A gift, by contrast, deliberately leaves something unsettled. The lingering sense of obligation is precisely what binds the parties together, so that an immediate and exactly equivalent return might even be regarded as an insult.

prompt: Why does the author describe the canoe voyages to exchange necklaces and armbands?
passage:
The Obligations of the Gift

In many societies, the exchange of gifts is far more than an expression of personal generosity. Early twentieth-century anthropologists, comparing accounts from Polynesia, Melanesia, and northwestern North America, argued that gifts are embedded in a system of three interlocking obligations: the obligation to give, the obligation to receive, and the obligation to reciprocate. Refusing a gift, in this view, is not a neutral act but a rejection of the social relationship it proposes, and failing to return one in due course can bring a loss of standing.

A celebrated example comes from the islands off the eastern tip of New Guinea, where men traditionally undertook long canoe voyages to exchange shell necklaces and armbands with partners on other islands. The objects had little practical use, and no participant kept them permanently; necklaces circulated in one direction around the ring of islands and armbands in the other. What the exchange produced, rather, was a durable web of partnerships that also facilitated more ordinary trade and cooperation.

Such cases have led scholars to distinguish gift economies from market exchange. In a market transaction, payment settles the account, and buyer and seller owe each other nothing further. A gift, by contrast, deliberately leaves something unsettled. The lingering sense of obligation is precisely what binds the parties together, so that an immediate and exactly equivalent return might even be regarded as an insult.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, which was a problem with traditional cargo handling?
passage:
The Container Revolution

For centuries, the loading and unloading of cargo ships was one of the most labor-intensive stages of international trade. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, crates, and bales of every size, and gangs of workers transferred them piece by piece between ships, warehouses, trucks, and railcars. A vessel might spend nearly as much time in port as at sea, and theft and damage were routine.

The adoption of standardized steel containers in the 1950s and 1960s transformed this system. Because every box conformed to the same dimensions and corner fittings, it could be lifted by crane directly from a truck to a ship and later onto a train without its contents ever being touched. Loading times fell from days to hours, and losses declined sharply. Achieving these gains, however, required more than the box itself. Ports had to invest heavily in specialized cranes and storage yards, shipping lines had to build new vessels, and competing firms had to agree on common specifications, a process that took years of negotiation.

The consequences extended well beyond the waterfront. As the cost of moving goods dropped, manufacturers could locate production far from their customers, and supply chains spanning several continents became economically viable. Meanwhile, many older harbors that lacked space for container terminals declined, while new ports emerged where land was plentiful.

choices.text: Ships often spent long periods waiting in port.

Workers refused to handle goods packed in barrels.

explanation: Paragraph 1 notes that a vessel might spend nearly as much time in port as at sea.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, why do individuals tend to overuse common resources?
passage:
Managing the Commons

Economists have long worried about the fate of resources that many people can use but no one owns, such as fishing grounds, grazing land, and groundwater. Because each user captures the full benefit of taking more while the cost of depletion is shared among everyone, individuals have an incentive to overuse the resource even when they recognize that collective restraint would leave them all better off. An influential essay published in 1968 popularized this dilemma as the "tragedy of the commons" and concluded that only two remedies were available: dividing the resource into private property or placing it under government regulation.

Subsequent fieldwork complicated this conclusion. Researchers documented numerous communities, from alpine villages that share mountain pastures to coastal groups that manage inshore fisheries, that had sustained common resources for generations without either privatization or central control. These arrangements were not matters of informal goodwill; they rested on designed institutions. Successful communities defined clearly who was entitled to use the resource, allowed users to participate in making and modifying the rules, monitored compliance, and imposed graduated penalties that grew more severe with repeated violations.

The findings did not show that collective management always succeeds. Self-governance tends to falter when user groups are large, when boundaries are hard to enforce, or when outsiders can exploit the resource. Nonetheless, they demonstrated that the choice between markets and states is not exhaustive.

Private owners compete with users for the same resource.

explanation: Paragraph 1 explains that each user captures the full benefit of taking more while depletion costs are shared.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what happens in the common laboratory procedure?
passage:
Change Blindness

Most people believe that they maintain a detailed and continuous picture of the scene in front of them. Experiments on what psychologists call change blindness suggest that this impression is largely an illusion. In a common laboratory procedure, observers view a photograph that alternates with a slightly altered version, separated by a brief blank screen. Even when the modification is substantial, such as a building vanishing from a skyline, many observers need dozens of cycles before they notice it, and some never do.

The blank interval is essential. Without it, the change produces a local flicker of motion that draws attention to the altered region. When that signal is masked, observers must compare the two images from memory, and their failures reveal how little of a scene is actually stored. Similar effects occur in everyday settings. In one field study, a researcher asking a pedestrian for directions was replaced by a different person during an interruption, and roughly half of the pedestrians failed to notice the switch.

These findings have prompted a reconsideration of how vision works. Rather than constructing a complete internal replica of the environment, the visual system may represent only the few objects currently receiving attention, relying on the world itself as an external memory. On this account, the sense of a richly detailed scene arises because information is available the moment we look for it.

explanation: Paragraph 1 states that many observers need dozens of cycles to notice a substantial change, and some never do.

The blank interval is essential. Without it, the change produces a local flicker of motion that draws attention to the altered region. When that signal is masked, observers must compare the two images from memory, and their failures reveal how little of a scene is actually stored. Similar effects occur in everyday settings. In one field study, a researcher asking a pedestrian for directions was replaced by a different person during an interruption, and roughly half of the pedestrians failed to notice the switch.

These findings have prompted a reconsideration of how vision works. Rather than constructing a complete internal replica of the environment, the visual system may represent only the few objects currently receiving attention, relying on the world itself as an external memory. On this account, the sense of a richly detailed scene arises because information is available the moment we look for it.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what were the main ingredients of Roman concrete?
passage:
The Secret of Roman Concrete

Many structures built by the ancient Romans are still standing after two thousand years, and much of their durability comes from a material known as Roman concrete. Unlike modern concrete, which is made with Portland cement, Roman concrete combined lime with a volcanic ash called pozzolana, along with chunks of rock or broken brick. When mixed with water, the lime and ash reacted to form a strong binding material that could harden even under water.

This property made Roman concrete especially valuable for harbor construction. Builders poured the mixture into wooden frames sunk into the sea, and over time, seawater actually strengthened the structures. Researchers studying ancient piers have found that salt water reacted with the volcanic ash to grow new minerals inside the concrete, filling small cracks before they could spread.

Modern concrete, by contrast, often weakens in seawater, partly because the steel bars placed inside it eventually rust and expand. For this reason, engineers have become interested in Roman techniques. Some laboratories are now testing mixtures that use volcanic ash or similar materials, hoping to produce concrete that lasts longer and requires less energy to manufacture. Ancient builders, it seems, may still have lessons to teach.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, why were very tall masonry buildings impractical?
passage:
How Buildings Learned to Rise

Before the late nineteenth century, the height of a building was limited by the thickness of its walls. In traditional masonry construction, the walls themselves carried the weight of every floor above, so the taller the building, the thicker its lower walls had to be. A sixteen-story masonry building completed in Chicago in 1891 required walls nearly two meters thick at its base, which consumed valuable space on the ground floor.

The solution was the metal frame. Instead of resting on the walls, the floors were attached to a skeleton of vertical columns and horizontal beams. The outer walls now carried only their own weight and could be made thin, with large windows. Chicago's Home Insurance Building, finished in 1885, is often cited as the first tall building to rely mainly on a metal frame, though historians still debate the title.

A frame alone, however, would not have made tall buildings practical. Few people were willing to climb ten or more flights of stairs every day. The safety elevator, which included a device that stopped the car if its cable broke, reassured the public that upper floors could be reached without danger. Together, the metal frame and the elevator transformed the skyline of the modern city.

Their stone was too expensive to transport to large cities.
Their walls could not be built higher than ten stories.
Their lower walls had to be so thick that they took up floor space.

explanation: Paragraph 1 explains that taller masonry buildings needed thicker lower walls, which consumed ground-floor space.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what was the main limitation of the harpsichord?
passage:
From Plucked Strings to Struck Strings

Before the piano was invented, the most common keyboard instrument in European homes was the harpsichord. When a player pressed a harpsichord key, a small quill plucked a string. The mechanism produced a bright, clear tone, but it had one important limitation: each string sounded at nearly the same volume no matter how hard or how softly the key was pressed.

Around 1700, an Italian instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori designed a keyboard in which small hammers struck the strings instead of plucking them. Because the force of each hammer depended on the player's touch, the instrument could produce both soft and loud notes. Cristofori's invention came to be called the pianoforte, from the Italian words for "soft" and "loud," a name later shortened to piano.

The early piano was much quieter than the modern instrument, and at first it spread slowly. Over the next century, however, makers strengthened its frame, added thicker strings, and eventually used iron to withstand the greater tension. These changes produced a fuller sound that could fill large concert halls. Composers responded by writing music with dramatic contrasts between gentle and powerful passages, effects that would have been impossible on the harpsichord. In this way, a mechanical improvement helped shape the style of music itself.

choices.text: Its volume could not be changed by the player's touch.
Its tone was too dull for performances at home.
Its strings broke easily when struck with force.
Its keys were too heavy for most players to press.

sampleAnswer: Its volume could not be changed by the player's touch.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the strings sounded at nearly the same volume no matter how hard the keys were pressed.

prompt: The word "precise" in the passage is closest in meaning to
passage:
Reading History in Tree Rings

Archaeologists often need to know exactly when a wooden building or object was made. One of the most precise methods for answering this question is dendrochronology, the study of tree rings. Each year, a tree in a temperate climate adds a new layer of wood, which appears as a ring when the trunk is cut. In a wet year the ring tends to be wide, while in a dry year it is narrow.

Because trees of the same species in a region experience similar weather, they record a similar pattern of wide and narrow rings. By comparing samples from living trees with samples from older timbers, researchers can match overlapping patterns and extend the record far into the past. In some parts of Europe, such sequences now reach back more than ten thousand years.

When archaeologists find a wooden beam in an ancient house, they can compare its ring pattern with this master sequence. If the outermost ring, just beneath the bark, has survived, the year the tree was cut can often be identified exactly. The method does have limits, however. Some species do not produce clear rings, and tropical trees, which grow throughout the year, are rarely useful. Even so, tree rings have dated sites ranging from prehistoric villages to medieval bridges.

passage:
Reading History in Tree Rings

Archaeologists often need to know exactly when a wooden building or object was made. One of the most precise methods for answering this question is dendrochronology, the study of tree rings. Each year, a tree in a temperate climate adds a new layer of wood, which appears as a ring when the trunk is cut. In a wet year the ring tends to be wide, while in a dry year it is narrow.

Because trees of the same species in a region experience similar weather, they record a similar pattern of wide and narrow rings. By comparing samples from living trees with samples from older timbers, researchers can match overlapping patterns and extend the record far into the past. In some parts of Europe, such sequences now reach back more than ten thousand years.

When archaeologists find a wooden beam in an ancient house, they can compare its ring pattern with this master sequence. If the outermost ring, just beneath the bark, has survived, the year the tree was cut can often be identified exactly. The method does have limits, however. Some species do not produce clear rings, and tropical trees, which grow throughout the year, are rarely useful. Even so, tree rings have dated sites ranging from prehistoric villages to medieval bridges.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what helped serialization become popular in Britain?
passage:
Novels in Installments

In the nineteenth century, many famous novels were not first published as complete books. Instead, they appeared in installments, a few chapters at a time, in magazines or in separate monthly parts. This practice, known as serialization, became especially popular in Britain after the 1830s, when cheaper printing and growing literacy created a large new audience of readers.

Serialization had clear advantages for both publishers and readers. A complete novel in three volumes was expensive, but a single monthly part cost only a small amount, so families who could never afford a full book could follow a story over many months. Publishers, for their part, received a steady income and could judge a story's popularity before investing in a bound edition.

The format also influenced how novels were written. Authors often ended an installment at a moment of suspense to make sure readers would buy the next one. Because they were sometimes writing only weeks ahead of publication, writers could respond to readers' letters and reviews, occasionally changing a character's fate in later chapters. Critics have argued that the long, crowded plots of many novels from this period, with their numerous characters and parallel storylines, are partly a product of this system. Readers today who open these books in a single volume are experiencing them in a way their first audiences did not.

Authors who refused to write novels in three volumes

explanation: Paragraph 1 says cheaper printing and growing literacy created a large new audience.

prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 1 about Brunelleschi's demonstration?
passage:
The Geometry of Seeing

Although painters in many cultures had developed ways of suggesting depth, the systematic technique known as linear perspective emerged in early fifteenth-century Florence. Its formulation is usually credited to the architect Filippo Brunelleschi, who reportedly demonstrated it with a painted panel of a city building viewed through a small hole, allowing observers to compare the image directly with the real scene. Some years later, the scholar Leon Battista Alberti codified the method in a treatise, giving painters a set of geometric rules rather than a single demonstration.

The principle underlying the technique is that parallel lines receding from the viewer appear to converge at a single vanishing point on the horizon, while objects diminish in size at a rate that can be calculated. Applying these rules allowed artists to construct a coherent pictorial space in which figures and buildings occupied consistent positions relative to one another and to the observer.

Historians have emphasized that this innovation was not merely technical. Linear perspective presupposes a fixed, singular viewpoint, effectively placing the spectator at the center of the represented world. Some scholars have therefore linked its adoption to a broader cultural interest in individual observation and measurement. Others caution against overstating the connection, noting that many painters treated the rules flexibly, deliberately distorting perspective when strict accuracy would have weakened a composition's emotional or narrative effect.

It was designed to teach painters a written set of rules.
It was meant to show that a constructed image could match a real view.
It was criticized by observers for distorting the building.

sampleAnswer: It was meant to show that a constructed image could match a real view.
explanation: Letting observers compare the panel directly with the real scene suggests its aim was to show the image matched reality.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, why did differences in local time cause little difficulty before the railroad?
passage:
Railroads and the Standardization of Time

Until the mid-nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, setting clocks so that noon corresponded to the moment the sun stood highest in the sky. Because the sun's position shifts gradually as one travels east or west, neighboring towns might differ by several minutes. For travelers moving on foot or by horse, such discrepancies were trivial, since no one could cover enough distance in a day for them to matter.

The railroad altered this situation fundamentally. A passenger could now pass through dozens of local times in a single journey, and railroad companies, each publishing schedules according to its own reference clock, compounded the confusion. More seriously, operating trains on shared single tracks required precise coordination; a discrepancy of a few minutes between two stations could put two trains on one track simultaneously.

In response, British railways adopted a uniform standard based on Greenwich time during the 1840s, and in 1883 railroads in the United States and Canada introduced a system of time zones, each spanning roughly fifteen degrees of longitude and differing from its neighbors by one hour. Notably, this reform was implemented by private companies rather than by governments; the United States did not make time zones official in federal law until 1918. The episode shows how a new technology can reshape something as seemingly natural as the measurement of a day.

Most towns agreed to follow the time of the nearest city.
Clocks were too inaccurate to show such small differences.
Few people needed to know the time of day precisely.

explanation: Paragraph 1 says no one could cover enough distance in a day for the discrepancies to matter.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, how did many earlier scholars view the repetitions in the Homeric epics?
passage:
Formulas and the Homeric Epics

For centuries, readers of the Homeric epics, the Iliad and the Odyssey, were puzzled by their frequent repetitions. Certain phrases, such as descriptions of the dawn or standard epithets attached to heroes' names, recur dozens of times, often in contexts where they seem only loosely relevant. Many scholars regarded these repetitions as stylistic flaws or as evidence that the poems had been assembled carelessly from earlier fragments.

In the 1920s and 1930s, the American scholar Milman Parry proposed a radically different explanation. He argued that the epics were products of an oral tradition in which poets composed while performing, without the aid of writing. To sustain a long narrative in strict meter, such poets relied on a vast stock of ready-made phrases, or formulas, each fitted to a particular position in the line. The repetitions, in this view, were not defects but essential tools of composition.

To test his hypothesis, Parry and his assistant Albert Lord recorded singers of epic poetry in the Balkans, some of whom could perform poems thousands of lines long. Their recordings revealed precisely the formulaic techniques Parry had inferred from the Greek texts. The theory has since been refined, and scholars still debate how the oral poems came to be written down and how much individual artistry they reflect. Nevertheless, Parry's work permanently changed how literary historians understand the relationship between memory, performance, and text.

As proof that the poems were composed orally
As the most beautiful passages in the poems
As later additions made by translators

explanation: Paragraph 1 says many scholars regarded the repetitions as stylistic flaws or evidence of careless assembly.

Many scholars regarded these repetitions as stylistic flaws or as evidence that the poems had been assembled carelessly from earlier fragments.

In the 1920s and 1930s, the American scholar Milman Parry proposed a radically different explanation. He argued that the epics were products of an oral tradition in which poets composed while performing, without the aid of writing. To sustain a long narrative in strict meter, such poets relied on a vast stock of ready-made phrases, or formulas, each fitted to a particular position in the line. The repetitions, in this view, were not defects but essential tools of composition.

To test his hypothesis, Parry and his assistant Albert Lord recorded singers of epic poetry in the Balkans, some of whom could perform poems thousands of lines long. Their recordings revealed precisely the formulaic techniques Parry had inferred from the Greek texts. The theory has since been refined, and scholars still debate how the oral poems came to be written down and how much individual artistry they reflect. Nevertheless, Parry's work permanently changed how literary historians understand the relationship between memory, performance, and text.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, what was the main obstacle to producing steel cheaply?
passage:
The Bessemer Process and Cheap Steel

Before the mid-nineteenth century, steel was a costly material produced in small quantities and reserved for items such as blades and springs. Most structural metal took the form of cast iron, which was strong under compression but brittle, or wrought iron, which was tougher but required laborious manual processing. The obstacle to producing steel cheaply lay in controlling carbon: pig iron from blast furnaces contained too much carbon, and removing the excess was slow and fuel-intensive.

In 1856, the English inventor Henry Bessemer patented a process that addressed this problem with surprising simplicity. Air was blown through molten pig iron in a large vessel called a converter. The oxygen combined with carbon and other impurities, and because these reactions released heat, the metal remained molten without additional fuel. Several tons of iron could now be converted in roughly twenty minutes, a task that had previously required many hours.

The early process was not without difficulties. Iron ores containing phosphorus yielded brittle steel, a problem not resolved until the late 1870s, when two British researchers developed a converter lining that absorbed phosphorus. Once this refinement made a wider range of ores usable, steel output expanded dramatically and prices fell steeply. Inexpensive steel subsequently made possible longer-lasting railroad rails, larger ships, and the frames of tall buildings, suggesting that a change in a single industrial step can ripple across an entire economy.

prompt: According to paragraph 1, why do archaeologists reproduce ancient technologies?
passage:
Experimental Archaeology

Archaeologists generally interpret the past through objects recovered from excavation, but artifacts alone rarely reveal how they were made or used. To address this gap, a field known as experimental archaeology attempts to reproduce ancient technologies under controlled conditions. Researchers might shape flint into stone tools, build replica houses using only materials available at the time, or smelt metal in reconstructed furnaces, recording each step in detail.

Such experiments can test hypotheses that would otherwise remain speculative. For example, by cutting meat and wood with replica stone tools and examining the resulting edges under a microscope, researchers have identified characteristic patterns of wear. These patterns can then be compared with those on ancient tools, allowing archaeologists to infer what a particular tool was used for. Similarly, deliberately burning reconstructed houses has shown investigators how the remains of a fire collapse and settle, helping them interpret burned structures at real sites.

Nonetheless, practitioners acknowledge important limitations. A successful replication shows only that a method was possible, not that ancient people actually used it. Modern experimenters also lack the years of practice that skilled craftspeople accumulated, so their results may underestimate what experienced workers could achieve. For these reasons, the most persuasive studies combine experimental results with other evidence, such as the distribution of finds at a site or residues preserved on artifacts, rather than treating replication as proof in itself.

choices.text: Excavations have become too expensive to carry out regularly.
Ancient objects are usually too fragile to be studied directly.
Museums need replicas to display instead of the originals.
Artifacts by themselves often do not show how they were made or used.

explanation: Paragraph 1 says artifacts alone rarely reveal how they were made or used, and experiments address this gap.

prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
audioScript:
Ryan: Professor Lindqvist, I'm worried about my replication project. The original study found that people remembered words better after drawing them, but my results showed no difference.
Professor Lindqvist: That's not necessarily a problem. Plenty of published effects don't hold up when someone repeats the study. Tell me about your participants.
Ryan: There were twenty-four, all from the same evening class. Most had been on campus since morning.
Professor Lindqvist: So they might have been tired, and twenty-four is fairly small. Either could hide a real effect, or the effect could be weaker than the original paper claimed.
Ryan: Should I recruit more people and run it again?
Professor Lindqvist: Not before the deadline. Report what you found honestly, and use your discussion section to explain those possible reasons.
Ryan: Okay. I guess I thought a result like this meant I'd made a mistake.
Professor Lindqvist: Not at all. A careful result that shows no effect is still evidence.

How to recruit more participants from evening classes
Whether the student can have more time for his project
