prompt: Dr. Chen: Since remote work became widespread, sociologists have begun examining its effects on local communities. On one hand, people who work from home spend more daytime hours in their own neighborhoods, potentially patronizing local businesses and getting to know neighbors. On the other hand, remote workers may become more isolated, interacting with colleagues only through screens and losing the casual social connections that offices once provided. In your view, has the growth of remote work strengthened or weakened people's sense of community? Support your answer with reasons or examples.
passage:
Ines: Remote work has strengthened neighborhood communities. When people commuted, residential areas were nearly empty during the day. Now, remote workers frequent local cafes, attend community events, and can volunteer at schools during flexible hours. I've noticed that neighbors on my street, who previously never spoke, now chat regularly while walking their dogs at lunchtime.

Oscar: Overall, I think remote work has weakened community. Workplaces were often where adults formed friendships across different backgrounds. Without that daily contact, many remote workers report loneliness, particularly young employees who recently moved to new cities and know nobody locally. Spending more time at home doesn't automatically translate into meaningful connections with neighbors.
sampleAnswer: I find Oscar's position somewhat more persuasive, although Ines describes a genuine benefit for certain neighborhoods. I suspect the effects of remote work depend heavily on a person's stage of life. Established residents with families and long-standing local ties may well become more involved in their neighborhoods, as Ines observes. However, young professionals who relocate for work often lack those ties, and the office previously served as their primary entry point into a new social world. My additional concern is that remote work reduces exposure to people unlike ourselves. Neighborhoods tend to be relatively homogeneous in terms of income and lifestyle, whereas workplaces bring together colleagues of different ages, cultures, and backgrounds. A cousin of mine who started a remote job after graduating spent months knowing almost no one in her new city. Community, therefore, has not simply moved from offices to neighborhoods; for many people, it has partially disappeared.

prompt: Dr. Duval: Traditional letter grades have been a fixture of higher education for over a century, but some institutions are experimenting with alternatives. These include pass/fail systems, in which students either meet course requirements or do not, and narrative evaluations, in which instructors write detailed comments describing each student's strengths and areas for growth. Advocates claim these alternatives reduce destructive competition and encourage intellectual risk-taking. Skeptics contend that they make it harder for employers and graduate programs to compare applicants. Should universities replace traditional letter grades with pass/fail or narrative evaluations? Explain your reasoning.
passage:
Naomi: Universities should move away from letter grades. Students today are so focused on protecting their grade point average that they avoid challenging courses outside their expertise. Narrative evaluations would encourage genuine curiosity and give students far more useful feedback than a single letter. A comment explaining how to strengthen an argument teaches much more than a B-minus.

Arjun: Letter grades should remain. They provide a clear, standardized signal that employers and admissions committees can interpret quickly. Without them, decision-makers may rely more heavily on factors like the prestige of a student's university or personal connections, which would disadvantage students from less privileged backgrounds. Grades, despite their flaws, offer a relatively objective measure.
sampleAnswer: Although Naomi presents an appealing vision of curiosity-driven learning, I agree with Arjun that letter grades should remain the primary system. His point about prestige is crucial: when standardized measures disappear, evaluators tend to substitute other signals, and those signals frequently favor students who already enjoy advantages. I would add that narrative evaluations raise practical concerns about consistency. Instructors differ enormously in their writing styles, and some are naturally generous with praise while others are reserved, so two equally capable students might receive descriptions that sound very different. Grades are imperfect, yet a common scale at least reduces this variation. That said, I believe universities could address Naomi's concern without eliminating grades entirely. Many institutions allow students to take one or two elective courses on a pass/fail basis, which encourages exploration while preserving reliable records. This compromise seems to combine the strengths of both approaches.

prompt: Dr. Park: Hiring practices vary considerably across organizations. Some employers prioritize demonstrated skills and experience, selecting candidates who can contribute effectively from their first day. Others emphasize potential, choosing applicants who may lack specific qualifications but show adaptability, curiosity, and a capacity for learning, and then investing in their training. Proponents of the latter approach argue that technical skills quickly become outdated in rapidly changing industries. When filling an important position, should companies prioritize candidates' current skills and experience or their long-term potential? Justify your view.
passage:
Hugo: Companies should prioritize proven skills and experience. Training inexperienced employees is costly and time-consuming, and there is no guarantee that potential will translate into actual performance. An experienced candidate has a track record that can be verified through references and past results, which significantly reduces the risk of a poor hiring decision for an important role.

Lina: Potential should be the priority. In industries like technology or marketing, the tools used today may be obsolete within five years, so an employee's ability to learn matters more than current expertise. Candidates selected for potential also tend to be highly motivated and loyal, since they appreciate the company's investment in their development.
sampleAnswer: While Hugo is right that experience reduces short-term risk, I am persuaded by Lina's argument that companies should prioritize long-term potential, particularly in rapidly evolving industries. Experience demonstrates what a candidate has accomplished under past conditions, but it reveals relatively little about how that person will respond to unfamiliar challenges. My additional reason is that hiring exclusively for experience can make organizations less diverse in their thinking. If every new employee comes from similar roles at competing firms, the company tends to replicate established practices rather than develop fresh approaches. Candidates with unconventional backgrounds often notice inefficiencies that industry veterans take for granted. For example, a friend of mine was hired by a logistics company after studying biology, and her experience with laboratory data led her to redesign the firm's inventory tracking system. Experience certainly matters, yet adaptability is what sustains an organization's performance over time.

prompt: Dr. Quinn: Ecotourism, defined as responsible travel to natural areas that supports conservation and local well-being, has expanded dramatically in recent decades. Advocates argue that it gives local communities a financial incentive to protect forests, reefs, and wildlife rather than exploit them, while educating visitors about environmental issues. Critics counter that growing numbers of tourists inevitably disturb wildlife, generate waste, and require roads and lodging that degrade the very environments they come to admire. On balance, do you believe ecotourism does more to protect or to harm fragile ecosystems? Explain your reasoning.
passage:
Camila: Ecotourism does more good than harm. Without tourism income, communities near rainforests often have little choice but to log or clear land for agriculture. When tourists pay to see intact ecosystems, preserving them becomes economically rational. Park entrance fees also fund rangers and research that governments might otherwise be unable to afford.

Nathan: I believe ecotourism ultimately causes more harm. Its popularity is self-defeating: as a destination becomes famous, visitor numbers grow beyond what the environment can support. Wildlife changes its behavior to avoid crowds, trails erode, and hotels strain local water supplies. Furthermore, the label ecotourism is often applied loosely to businesses with minimal environmental commitments.
sampleAnswer: I believe ecotourism does more to protect fragile ecosystems, provided it is properly regulated, and in this respect I agree with Camila's argument about economic incentives. Nathan correctly warns that popularity can become self-defeating, but I see this as a problem of management rather than an inherent flaw. Destinations that cap daily visitor numbers, require licensed guides, and restrict construction have demonstrated that tourism and conservation can coexist. My additional point concerns the alternatives. If a forest generates no tourism income, it is rarely left untouched; more often, it faces pressure from mining, logging, or large-scale agriculture, all of which cause far more permanent damage than visitors on guided trails. Moreover, ecotourism creates a constituency of people who have personally witnessed these ecosystems and are therefore more likely to support their protection after returning home. Responsible tourism is often the most realistic way to make conservation financially sustainable.

prompt: Dr. Osei: Sleep researchers have found that adolescents' internal clocks shift during puberty, making it biologically difficult for many teenagers to fall asleep before eleven at night. Nevertheless, numerous high schools begin classes before eight in the morning, and chronic sleep deprivation among teenagers has been linked to poorer academic performance, mood problems, and car accidents. Some school districts have delayed start times, but opponents point to complications involving bus schedules, after-school sports, and parents' work hours. Should high schools adopt later start times to accommodate adolescent sleep patterns? Explain your position.
passage:
Maya: High schools should definitely start later. The scientific evidence is compelling, and it would be unreasonable to ignore students' biology for the sake of convenience. Districts that have shifted start times have reported improvements in attendance and alertness. The logistical challenges with buses and sports are real, but they are solvable problems, whereas sleep deprivation harms students' health directly.

Ryan: I'm skeptical that later start times are the right solution. If school begins later, it ends later, which pushes sports, part-time jobs, and homework further into the evening. Many teenagers might simply go to bed later still, eliminating the benefit. Schools would achieve more by educating families about limiting screen use at night and maintaining consistent sleep schedules.
sampleAnswer: I support later start times, and I find Maya's argument more convincing than Ryan's, though Ryan raises a reasonable concern about evening schedules. The crucial distinction is that education about screen use, while valuable, asks teenagers to override a biological shift that the research describes as genuinely difficult to resist. Expecting individual willpower to overcome biology seems less realistic than adjusting an institutional schedule. My additional reason concerns fairness. Students from families with flexible resources can compensate for early start times, for instance by being driven to school rather than catching a bus before dawn. Students without those options bear the full burden of sleep loss, which may widen existing gaps in academic achievement. As for Ryan's worry that teenagers will simply stay up later, studies of districts that changed their schedules found that students gained sleep overall. Therefore, although implementation requires careful planning, the health benefits justify the change.

prompt: Dr. Lindgren: Most social media platforms now arrange posts using recommendation algorithms, which predict what each user is most likely to engage with, rather than displaying posts in chronological order. Platforms argue that algorithmic feeds help users find relevant content amid overwhelming volume. Critics contend that these systems prioritize content that provokes strong emotional reactions, encourage compulsive scrolling, and give users little control over what they see. Some researchers have proposed requiring platforms to offer a simple chronological feed as the default option. Do you think social media platforms should make chronological feeds the default? Why or why not?
passage:
Keira: Chronological feeds should be the default. Algorithms are designed to maximize the time users spend on a platform, not their well-being. A chronological feed restores user control: people see posts from accounts they deliberately chose to follow, in the order they appeared, and can stop scrolling once they've caught up. Transparency like this builds healthier online habits.

Mateo: I don't think chronological feeds should be the default. Most users follow hundreds of accounts, so a purely chronological feed would bury important posts, like a close friend's news, beneath a flood of minor updates. Recommendation systems, despite their flaws, solve a genuine problem of information overload. Users who prefer chronological order can already switch settings on many platforms.
sampleAnswer: Although Mateo makes a fair point about information overload, I agree with Keira that chronological feeds should be the default. Mateo notes that users can already change their settings, but research on default options suggests that most people never alter them, so the default effectively determines the experience of the majority. Given this influence, defaults should favor transparency and user control rather than the platform's commercial interest in maximizing engagement. My additional argument is that a chronological feed gives users a clear sense of completion. With an algorithmic feed, content never runs out, which encourages the compulsive scrolling Keira mentions. When I switched one of my accounts to chronological order, I found that I checked it less frequently and ended each session feeling informed rather than drained.
